en.title: GTA 6 extended look: What we know after Netflix preview
en.description: After more than 18 months since the last official glimpse of Grand Theft Auto 6, developer Rockstar has shown fans a 26-minute preview of the upcom...
en.fullContent:
After more than 18 months since the last official glimpse of Grand Theft Auto 6, developer Rockstar has shown fans a 26-minute preview of the upcoming blockbuster video game.

Its "extended look" debuted on Netflix, six hours before going live on YouTube, and was the first chance players have had to see detailed footage of the title in action.

The montage, with no commentary or explanatory captions, showed off improved graphics, detailed environments and a selection of car-chases and shoot-outs from the sequel.

The broadcast followed a week of unauthorised gameplay leaks, which the developer said it had been "heartbreaking" to see shared online.

After it got its chance to show the version of GTA 6 it wanted the world to see, here are some things we learned, and some things we still don't know.

The extended look spent a long time showcasing the relationship between protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino, the couple at the centre of GTA 6's "Bonnie and Clyde" story.

en.title: Gamescom: Germany is Europe’s largest video game market
en.description: Packed exhibition halls in Cologne are a given at Gamescom these days. People's leisure habits in Germany have changed markedly over the past ten y...
en.fullContent:
Packed exhibition halls in Cologne are a given at Gamescom these days. People's leisure habits in Germany have changed markedly over the past ten years and become increasingly digital.

Today, 33 percent of respondents in the latest so-called "Leisure Monitor" say they play video games at least once a week. Only smartphone activities and listening to music have seen even stronger growth.

This year's Gamescom, which was expected to attract more than 350,000 visitors, is being held under the slogan "Games whet the appetite for the future." Henna Virkkunen, vice-president of the European Commission responsible for digital technologies, is also coming to Cologne to talk about the European Union's strategy on games. The EU commissioner will meet Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, Research Minister Dorothee Bar and North Rhine-Westphalia state premier Hendrik Wust.

Today, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will become the first German president ever to visit Gamescom, where he will open the Gamescom congress.

According to the 2026 annual report on Germany's games industry, revenue from games, games hardware and online gaming services in Germany reached around €9.4 billion in 2025. That represents growth of 4 percent compared with the previous year. This makes Germany the largest games market in Europe and the fifth-largest worldwide.

Industry representatives in Germany are correspondingly confident: “As the world’s biggest games event, Gamescom is once again making one thing abundantly clear this year: we need to make far better use of the unique potential of games and their cultural, economic and technological power. It must be Germany’s and Europe’s ambition to play a leading role as a production hub for games,” said Game managing director Felix Falk ahead of the trade fair.

en.title: RIP Tim Curry, Video Game (And Regular) Actor Extraordinaire
en.description: Because this week evidently decided it hadn’t already taken enough beloved 80-year-olds from us, Tim Curry passed away Tuesday night. A king of cam...
en.fullContent:
Because this week evidently decided it hadn’t already taken enough beloved 80-year-olds from us, Tim Curry passed away Tuesday night. A king of camp, many remember Curry for scene-stealing roles in movies like Clue, The Rocky Horror Picture Show, and of course, Muppet Treasure Island. But he also loved popping up in video games, a perfect fit for his inimitably over-the-top stylings.

According to Moby Games, Curry ultimately appeared in 22 games. While some of these were licensed fare—Curry voiced Nigel Thornberry in The Wild Thornberrys, after all—his gameography is littered with heavy hitters including Gabriel Knight, Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger, Brütal Legend, Dragon Age: Origins, and Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3. The latter role pretty much guarantees Curry’s immortality all by itself thanks to a line read so good that Vice dedicated a whole oral history to it.

“I’m escaping to the one place that hasn’t been corrupted by capitalism,” Curry, as Premier Anatoly Cherdenko, bellows, half-panting, half-convulsing with unbridled enthusiasm. Then he blurts the piece de resistance so hard that you can practically feel his spittle on your face: “Space!”

“He didn't die, he simply escaped to the one place that hasn't been corrupted by capitalism,” reads a comment made today on a YouTube video of the clip, echoing the same sentiment as countless others.

In honor of a man who could bring gravitas even to the silliest moments, here’s more highlights from Curry’s video game voice (and regular) acting career:

That Dragon Age clip, especially, suggests that even as somebody who came up before video games exploded into a multibillion-dollar industry, game roles weren’t just a job to Curry; he found them legitimately interesting.

en.title: My Son Has Found an Innovative Way to Play an Online Video Game. I’m Worried About What This Says About Him.
en.description: Care and Feeding is Slate’s parenting advice column. Have a question for Care and Feeding? Submit it here.
en.fullContent:
Care and Feeding is Slate’s parenting advice column. Have a question for Care and Feeding? Submit it here.

I have a 14-year-old son, “Kevin.” He’s gotten into this online multiplayer game. He’s not letting it consume his life, he still does well on his school and other activities, but some of his actions within the game have made me both proud of his successes and worried about them at the same time.

The game itself is a kind of a very long scale, vaguely medieval fantasy thing. You found an estate, you get resources from it, you improve your resources by building various things on your estate, and you raise troops. It’s very hard to directly damage someone else’s estate, but you can raid them for resources, and this is apparently very common. You’re frequently engaged in an all-against-all war of cattle, crystal, and grain theft, and shifting alliances of raiding each other seem to be what most of the game is about.

Kevin has created a new model for his own playing strategy, and it seems to be working. Instead of simply raiding other people, he’s offered them the opportunity to become a “client.” Clientage does require ongoing protection payments, but he actually does provide protection. If anyone else raids you or demands tribute, he’ll start attacking whoever is bothering his clients, even if it’s an economic loser to fight against a stronger opponent. And he’s started coordinating the raiding efforts of his client base in order to present united fronts against threats and dogpile on the player he’s selected as the next person to recruit in.

But it is working. He was so excited when he checked his messages after school and he had two people asking to be his clients that he hadn’t even raided them to “convince” them to sign up.

So I’m both proud of his skills—he clearly is engaging with the game strategically—but I’m also worried that he’s independently recreated the logic of the protection racket. Is this something I should be taking steps about?

en.title: Dear Abby: My fiancé spends all night playing video games — it’s killing our relationship
en.description: DEAR ABBY: My fiance, “Dustin,” and I have been a couple for five years. We live together and are fairly happy. The problem is his gaming habits. A...
en.fullContent:
DEAR ABBY: My fiance, “Dustin,” and I have been a couple for five years. We live together and are fairly happy. The problem is his gaming habits. At first, it wasn’t an issue because I also play the occasional video game. Since moving into our own place, I’ve noticed Dustin has started spending a tremendous amount of time on these video games. From the time he wakes up around 1 p.m. until right after he gets off work around 10 p.m., he’ll log on and play for hours. Most nights he doesn’t come to bed until 5 a.m.!

With all his free time, he doesn’t help clean or cook, and I get none of his attention. I’m not sure where I go from here. I have spoken to him about this habit, but he doesn’t see any issue because he grew up constantly playing games. I need some guidance on this issue because it’s driving a wedge in our relationship. — GAME OVER IN NORTH CAROLINA

DEAR GAME OVER: Dustin doesn’t see any issue with the status quo because it isn’t a problem — for him. He’s got a pretty good deal. You do the cooking and the cleaning and contribute to half the expenses, but you’re not even getting companionship.

Tell your fiance you need more from him because this isn’t what you signed up for when you moved in together. Offer him the option of couples counseling so your issues can be mediated. If he isn’t willing and this doesn’t resolve the problem, then cut your losses and move out unless you want to spend the rest of your life as a “gaming widow.”

DEAR ABBY: My middle-aged son is on the autism spectrum and has recently come back home to live with us. He left home at 19 and has always had roommates. We didn’t realize that he had autism until about a year ago.

We like having him here but are having a difficult time adjusting. My son has agreed to help with bills and contribute toward groceries, but my husband thinks we should split all expenses three ways equally. My son works in the food service industry and earns a low wage, even though he puts in 32 to 34 hours a week. He eats at work most of the time and at home only twice a week. I’m retired and live on a small Social Security check. My husband makes more than twice what my son and I make.
